:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = 2x^2 - xy - z^2,$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)$ can be found by computing 
$\nabla f(2, 3, \sqrt 2).$   

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j-2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,\sqrt{2}) & =(4\cdot 2-3)\text{ }i-2\text{ }j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5i-2j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $5 \mathbf i  - 2 \mathbf j - 2 \sqrt 2\ \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $4\,i+j+4\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-2yz+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,k \\  & ={y}^{2}\text{ }i+(2xy-2z)\text{ }j+(-2y+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,1) & =(-1)^{2}\,i+(2(1)(-1)-2(1))\,j+(-2(-1)+1)\,k \\  & =1\,i-4j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $\,i-4\,j+3\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,4,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz})\,k \\  & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}}\,i+(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}}+\frac{z}{2\sqrt{yz}})j+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{yz}}\,k \\ ∇f(1,4,1) & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{1(4)}}\,i+(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1(4)}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4(1)}})j+\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(1)}}\,k \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,1,-1).$  

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,k \\  & =({y}^{2}+2xz)\text{ }i+(2xy+{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2yz+{x}^{2})\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,1,-1) & =((1)^{2}+2(-1)(-1))\,i+(2(-1)(1)+(-1)^{2}))\,j+(2(1)(-1)+(-1)^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i-1j-1\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $3\,i-\,j-\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,k \\  & =-\frac{y}{{z}^{2}-xy}\text{ }i+(-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}-xy}-z)\text{ }j+(\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}-xy}-y)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =-\frac{(-2)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}\,i+(-\frac{1}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-0)\,j+(\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-(-2))\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(0,0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+y{e}^{z}+z{e}^{x})\,k \\  & =({e}^{y}+z{e}^{x})\,i+(x{e}^{y}+{e}^{z})\,j+(y{e}^{z}+{e}^{x})\,k \\ ∇f(0,0,1) & =({e}^{0}+(1){e}^{0})i+((0){e}^{0}+{e}^{1})j+((0){e}^{1}+{e}^{0})k \\  & =2\,i+e\,j+k\end{aligned}

Therefore, $2\,i+e\,j+k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(0,0,1).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(3{x}^{2}yz-y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{3}z-x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+({x}^{3}y-2xyz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,1) & =(3(1)^{2}(-2)(1)-(-2)(1)^{2})\,i+((1)^{3}(1)-(1)(1)^{2})\,j+((1)^{3}(-2)-2(1)(-2)(1))\,k \\  & =-4\,i+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-4\,i+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,1).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,k \\  & =3{x}^{2}\text{ }i+2{z}^{2}y\text{ }j+(2z{y}^{2}+2)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,-1) & =3(1)^{2}\,i+2(-1)^{2}(-1)\,j+(2(-1)(-1)^{2}+2)k \\  & =3\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,0,1) & =2(-1)\,i+2(0)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-2\,i+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-2\,i+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1).$

$∇f(0,0,0).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-2,-3,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-2,-3,1) & =(4(-2)-(-3))\,i-(-2)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
